title: Antibodies, Complement, Infectious Immunity and Hypersensitivity — DOMiNANCE Originals
source: KNUST Immunology lectures and Hypersensitivity Reactions study guide

questions.stem: How many heavy and light chains form the basic antibody monomer?

options.label: A
options.text: One heavy and two light chains

options.label: B
options.text: Two heavy and one light chain

options.label: C
options.text: Three heavy and one light chain

options.label: D
options.text: Two heavy and two light chains

options.label: E
options.text: Four heavy and no light chains

questions.why: A conventional immunoglobulin monomer has two identical heavy and two identical light chains linked by disulphide bonds.

questions.stem: Which antibody region largely determines antigen-binding specificity?

options.label: A
options.text: Constant domains of both heavy chains

options.label: B
options.text: Variable regions in both chain types

options.label: C
options.text: Carbohydrate coating of the Fc region

options.label: D
options.text: Terminal region of the J chain

questions.why: The antigen-binding site is formed by variable-region domains of heavy and light chains.

questions.stem: Which immunoglobulin class is usually most abundant in adult serum?
questions.why: IgG typically represents the largest proportion of circulating immunoglobulin.

questions.stem: Which immunoglobulin normally crosses the placenta to provide passive fetal immunity?
questions.why: FcRn-mediated transport permits maternal IgG to enter fetal circulation.

questions.stem: Which immunoglobulin is a useful marker of a recent primary immune response?
questions.why: IgM is often produced early in a primary antibody response and can suggest recent infection.

questions.stem: Which antibody is characteristically present as a J-chain-linked pentamer in plasma?
questions.why: Secreted IgM typically has a pentameric architecture, providing high avidity for multivalent antigen.

questions.stem: Which antibody class is typically dimeric in mucosal secretions?
questions.why: Secretory IgA contains a J-chain-linked dimer and secretory component for mucosal protection.

questions.stem: Which immunoglobulin has high-affinity binding to mast-cell Fc receptors in immediate allergy?
questions.why: IgE binds FcεRI on mast cells and basophils, enabling rapid allergen-triggered degranulation.

questions.stem: Which immunoglobulin is commonly expressed with IgM on naive mature B-cell surfaces?
questions.why: Membrane IgD and IgM can function as antigen receptors on mature naive B cells.

questions.stem: Which antibody fragment retains the principal antigen-binding sites after proteolytic cleavage?
questions.why: Fab comprises antibody antigen-binding arms; Fc contributes effector functions and receptor interactions.

questions.stem: Why does IgM often strongly activate complement during a primary immune response?

options.label: A
options.text: Its Fc region directly cleaves C3

options.label: C
options.text: It activates only the lectin route

options.label: E
options.text: Its J chain acts as a membrane pore

questions.why: Antigen-bound IgM presents a multivalent geometry favourable for classical-pathway activation.

questions.stem: How does a monoclonal antibody preparation differ from a conventional polyclonal antiserum?

options.label: A
options.text: It contains all antibody clones from serum

options.label: B
options.text: It recognizes one defined epitope specificity

options.label: C
options.text: It binds every epitope on one protein

options.label: D
options.text: It cannot recognize any protein antigen

options.label: E
options.text: It lacks an immunoglobulin Fc region

questions.why: Monoclonal antibodies derive from one antibody-producing clone and generally have a single specificity.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of fusing an antibody-producing B cell with a myeloma cell?
questions.why: Hybridomas combine B-cell antibody specificity with the capacity for continuous proliferation.

questions.stem: Why are unfused myeloma cells unable to persist in aminopterin-containing HAT medium when salvage-deficient?

options.label: C
options.text: They cannot salvage nucleotides under HAT

options.label: E
options.text: They cannot synthesize any nuclear proteins

questions.why: Aminopterin blocks de novo nucleotide synthesis; salvage-deficient myeloma cells cannot survive HAT selection.

questions.stem: Which HAT medium component directly blocks de novo nucleotide synthesis?
questions.why: Aminopterin inhibits folate-dependent nucleotide synthesis, making salvage-dependent selection possible.

questions.stem: Which monoclonal antibody design contains murine variable regions joined to human constant regions?
questions.why: Chimeric antibodies retain mouse-derived variable domains but have human constant regions.

questions.stem: Which antibody design typically retains mainly murine complementarity-determining regions in a human framework?
questions.why: Humanization usually grafts mouse antigen-binding loops onto largely human antibody frameworks.

questions.stem: What distinguishes a conjugated monoclonal antibody from a naked monoclonal antibody?

options.label: E
options.text: An attached drug or radioactive payload

questions.why: Conjugated mAbs are linked to therapeutic payloads, whereas naked mAbs act without such attached agents.

questions.stem: What allows a bispecific antibody to bring two different targets into proximity?

options.label: E
options.text: Two covalently attached vitamin K groups

questions.why: Bispecific antibodies are engineered to bind different targets, such as a tumour antigen and T-cell CD3.

questions.stem: Which event initiates the classical complement pathway most directly?
questions.why: C1q binds appropriately clustered IgG or IgM Fc regions on antigen, initiating the classical cascade.

questions.stem: Which complex functions as the classical-pathway C3 convertase?
questions.why: Classical and lectin pathways generate the C4b2a C3 convertase.

questions.stem: Which complex functions as the alternative-pathway C3 convertase?
questions.why: Alternative pathway C3 convertase is the C3bBb complex stabilized by properdin.

questions.stem: Which plasma enzyme cleaves factor B after it binds C3b in the alternative pathway?
questions.why: Factor D cleaves C3b-bound factor B to generate the active Bb-containing convertase.

questions.stem: Which lectin pathway protein recognizes microbial mannose-rich carbohydrates?
questions.why: MBL binds microbial carbohydrates, recruiting MASP proteases to initiate lectin-pathway complement activation.

questions.stem: Which complement fragment binds microbial surfaces and enhances their phagocytic uptake?
questions.why: C3b acts as an important opsonin recognized by phagocyte complement receptors.

questions.stem: Which complement fragment is a potent chemoattractant and inflammatory mediator?
questions.why: C5a promotes leukocyte recruitment and activation and is an anaphylatoxin.

questions.stem: Which group of components forms the terminal membrane attack complex?
questions.why: C5b recruits C6, C7, C8 and polymerizing C9 to form membrane-disrupting pores.

questions.stem: Which complement pathway can be initiated on microbial surfaces without antigen-specific antibody?
questions.why: Alternative-pathway tick-over and surface amplification can operate independently of antibodies.

questions.stem: What is the principal difference between classical and lectin complement activation at the initiating step?

options.label: D
options.text: MHC class I versus MHC class II

questions.why: Classical activation begins with C1 bound to antibody; lectin activation begins with MBL/ficolin recognition of microbial sugars.

questions.stem: Why may serum complement C3 and C4 concentrations fall during active immune-complex disease?

options.label: B
options.text: The immune complexes permanently synthesize C3

options.label: C
options.text: C3b directly prevents hepatic albumin production

options.label: E
options.text: The immune complexes suppress every cytokine

questions.why: Ongoing complement activation consumes circulating proteins, which may lower serum C3 and C4.

questions.stem: Which laboratory assay evaluates activity of the classical complement pathway as a functional unit?
questions.why: CH50 tests complement-mediated lysis requiring an intact classical-to-terminal pathway.

questions.stem: Which innate cytokines help establish an antiviral state in nearby uninfected cells?
questions.why: Interferon-alpha and beta induce antiviral gene programs that limit viral replication.

questions.stem: Which lymphocytes can rapidly attack virus-infected cells before a fully specific T-cell response develops?
questions.why: NK cells provide an early innate cytotoxic response to infected or stressed cells.

questions.stem: Which adaptive mechanism most directly destroys host cells containing replicating viruses?
questions.why: CD8 T lymphocytes recognize viral peptides on MHC I and kill infected host cells.

questions.stem: Which immune mechanism primarily prevents extracellular viruses from attaching to target cells?
questions.why: Neutralizing antibodies bind virions and can block receptor engagement and entry.

questions.stem: Which response is particularly effective against encapsulated extracellular bacteria?

options.label: A
options.text: CD8 killing of uninfected epithelial cells

questions.why: IgG/C3b-mediated opsonization facilitates neutrophil and macrophage uptake of extracellular bacteria.

questions.stem: Which adaptive pathway is especially important against bacteria surviving within macrophages?

options.label: C
options.text: IgE stimulation of mast cells only

questions.why: Th1-derived IFN-γ enhances macrophage killing of intracellular pathogens such as mycobacteria.

questions.stem: A mycobacterium prevents phagosome–lysosome fusion. What defence is thereby evaded?

options.label: B
options.text: Direct lysis by red blood cells

questions.why: Preventing phagolysosomal maturation allows survival within phagocytes.

questions.stem: Which response is most strongly associated with defence against helminths?

options.label: A
options.text: Th1, IgG and cytotoxic CD8 cells

options.label: B
options.text: Type I interferons and NK cells

questions.why: Helminth defence involves Th2 cytokines, IgE and eosinophil-mediated effector mechanisms.

questions.stem: Which immune cells are prominent in acute defence against many invasive fungal infections?
questions.why: Innate phagocytes are crucial for fungal defence; neutropenia greatly increases invasive fungal risk.

questions.stem: Why does antigenic variation favour viral persistence or reinfection?

options.label: B
options.text: It disables every innate interferon receptor

options.label: C
options.text: It prevents all replication of viral genomes

options.label: D
options.text: It reduces recognition by existing immunity

questions.why: Changes in viral epitopes can reduce neutralization or T-cell recognition by previously generated responses.

questions.stem: Which immunological mechanism defines type I immediate hypersensitivity?
questions.why: Type I reactions involve IgE bound to FcεRI on mast cells and basophils.

questions.stem: Why may a first allergen encounter produce no immediate symptoms but later exposure causes hives?

options.label: A
options.text: First exposure depletes every mast cell

options.label: B
options.text: Allergen must first mutate within plasma

options.label: C
options.text: Allergens require a complement C9 pore

questions.why: Initial exposure can induce IgE production and mast-cell sensitization; subsequent crosslinking triggers degranulation.

questions.stem: Which event directly triggers degranulation of sensitized mast cells during re-exposure?

options.label: B
options.text: Binding of IgM to erythrocyte antigen

options.label: D
options.text: Formation of memory CD8 T cells

questions.why: Allergen crosslinks FcεRI-bound IgE molecules, activating the mast cell.

questions.stem: Which mediator is preformed in mast-cell granules and rapidly causes vascular permeability?
questions.why: Histamine is stored and released immediately; lipid mediators such as leukotrienes are synthesized after activation.

questions.stem: Which treatment is first-line for life-threatening systemic anaphylaxis?
questions.why: Intramuscular adrenaline rapidly treats vasodilation and bronchospasm; antihistamines and steroids are adjuncts.

questions.stem: Which test produces a wheal-and-flare reaction within minutes in a sensitized person?
questions.why: Immediate wheal-and-flare reflects mast-cell IgE-dependent histamine release.

questions.stem: Which mechanism is characteristic of type II hypersensitivity?

options.label: B
options.text: CD4 T cells respond after two days

options.label: E
options.text: Antibody binds a fixed cell-surface target

questions.why: Type II reactions involve IgG/IgM directed against cell or matrix antigens and may cause destruction or receptor dysfunction.

questions.stem: Why can Graves disease be classified as receptor-mediated type II hypersensitivity?

options.label: D
options.text: CD8 cells remove all thyroid follicles

questions.why: TSH receptor-stimulating autoantibodies produce inappropriate receptor signalling.

questions.stem: Which disease illustrates receptor-blocking rather than receptor-stimulating type II hypersensitivity?
questions.why: Myasthenia gravis antibodies commonly impair neuromuscular acetylcholine receptor function.

questions.stem: Which laboratory test detects immunoglobulin already bound to erythrocytes in vivo?
questions.why: The direct Coombs test detects antibody or complement coating circulating red blood cells.

questions.stem: Which immunological event initiates type III hypersensitivity injury?

options.label: A
options.text: Direct IgG binding to a cell receptor

options.label: C
options.text: Cross-linking of IgE on mast cells

options.label: D
options.text: CD8 T-cell recognition of host peptides

questions.why: Type III lesions result from circulating or locally formed immune complexes depositing in tissues and activating complement.

questions.stem: A patient develops fever, arthralgia and rash several days after exposure to foreign serum proteins. What mechanism is likely?
questions.why: Serum sickness is a systemic type III immune-complex reaction.

questions.stem: What is an Arthus reaction?
questions.why: An Arthus reaction results from local immune-complex formation in previously sensitized tissue.

questions.stem: Which renal immunofluorescence pattern is typical of immune-complex glomerulonephritis?
questions.why: Type III immune-complex deposition often produces a granular staining pattern, unlike linear anti-basement-membrane antibodies.

questions.stem: Which disease is a classical example of type II antibody binding directly to a basement-membrane antigen?
questions.why: Anti-GBM antibodies bind basement-membrane antigens directly, producing a linear immunofluorescence pattern.

questions.stem: What is the principal mediator of type IV delayed hypersensitivity?
questions.why: Type IV hypersensitivity is T-cell mediated rather than primarily antibody mediated.

questions.stem: When does a typical tuberculin delayed-type skin reaction peak?
questions.why: Delayed type IV reactions commonly become prominent over 48–72 hours as memory T cells recruit inflammatory cells.

questions.stem: Which condition best represents a contact dermatitis mediated by type IV hypersensitivity?
questions.why: Contact hypersensitivity to nickel is mainly a delayed T-cell-mediated reaction.

questions.stem: Which cells most directly mediate tissue injury in a classic Th1-type delayed reaction?
questions.why: Previously sensitized Th1 cells release cytokines that recruit and activate macrophages, producing delayed inflammation.
